name: Bronze Green
lede: Bronze green is a dark grey-green, and in old paint catalogs it was the trade name of cheap mixed greens rather than of one pigment.

sections.title: A trade name
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium traces the name through several sources that do not agree [1]. Salter, in 1869, called bronze a species of Prussian green, a dull blue-black that looks greenish black with a coppery cast in deep washes [1]. Linke and Adam, in 1913, list it as a trade name for cinnabar green or chrome green [1].

Rose, in 1916, uses it for various cheap greens made with ochre, coal, Berlin blue or ultramarine, and for a blend of chrome yellow with a blue and black [1]. Heaton, in 1928, calls it a current synonym for a variety of [[brunswick-green]], and Winsor and Newton used it in 1938 as a watercolor name for a mixed chrome green [1].

sections.title: A recipe, and industrial paint
sections.body:
Mierzinski, in 1881, gives a recipe: 100 parts of chrome yellow, 100 of zinc white, 6 of Berlin blue and 6 of black [1]. Rivington, in 1901, lists bronze-green as one of three colors, with chocolate and black, of an enamel paint for industrial surfaces [1]. So the color was as much a workshop and railing color as an artist's one.

The swatch is a dark, muted green close to [[bronze]], [[moss-green]] and [[olive]], and far greener than the blue of [[prussian-blue]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds it in 758 of 23,781 paintings, 3.19 percent, as photographed [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 40 percent of the 431 paintings where the within-painting lens finds it [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 77 of 1,674 paintings, about 2.4 times the baseline [2]. The most devoted painter is Harald Giersing, in 6 of 23 works here [2]. Photographs of aged, varnished paintings cannot tell a pigment from a dark green mixture [2].
